3.3 — Fire Rate: Cooldowns & Time

Last lesson you pressed Play, walked into range, and the turret did not fire a shot — it fired a stream. Nothing you wrote is broken. Your range check runs every frame, and every frame it called your firing method, so the turret has been firing at your frame rate. Today you fix that. The fix has more than one honest answer, and you are going to pick one and defend it.

The Problem: An Action That Happens Too Often ~15 min

Rate limiting is a problem software has solved in every domain: a login form that must not accept a thousand attempts a second, a printer that must not accept a thousand jobs, a turret that must not fire a thousand bullets. The shape of the solution is always the same — remember when the last one happened, and refuse until enough time has passed — but the engine gives you several ways to remember.

Before you pick one, notice what you cannot do. Update() is called by the engine every frame; there is no way to make it "wait". Any pause you write has to be a test that fails for a while, not a stop.

ApproachWhat you storeThe gateWhat it costs you
(a) A Time.time timestamp One float: the moment the last shot happened. Time.time >= lastShot + cooldown One line of state. Forgetting to write the new timestamp turns the gate permanently true — you get the frame-rate bug straight back. A timestamp is only meaningful against the same clock, so anything that pauses or resets time needs thought.
(b) A countdown timer One float: seconds remaining until the next shot is allowed. timer <= 0f, then timer = cooldown The timer must be decremented by Time.deltaTime on every frame, including frames where the turret is not firing. Forget that and the number quietly stops meaning anything. In exchange, the field reads as "seconds until I can shoot" — which is exactly what a designer wants to see.
(c) InvokeRepeating Nothing at all — the engine holds the schedule. InvokeRepeating(nameof(Fire), 0f, cooldown) Almost no code, and that is the trap: the engine keeps calling your method on cadence whether or not the player is in range, so you still need a range check inside the method. Cancelling is by method name, so renaming the method breaks the cancel silently. Re-tuning the rate at runtime means cancelling and re-invoking.
(d) A coroutine loop A running coroutine handle. while (true) { yield return new WaitForSeconds(t); } The most powerful and the most readable for sequences, and the only one that expresses "charge, then burst, then rest" cleanly. It costs you a StartCoroutine call, a stored handle to stop it, and a second mental model of when your code runs.
These are not ranked — they are priced. Every row above is used in real shipped games. The question is never "which is correct", it is "which cost am I willing to pay for this behaviour, in this project, this week". Row (a) is the cheapest thing that works. Row (d) is the right tool the moment a single cooldown is not enough to describe the behaviour. Rows (b) and (c) sit between them.
Where this sits in your existing design. In 3.1 you made detection a condition that is re-evaluated every frame, not an event — and you were told that would matter. Here it is. A condition that is true for sixty consecutive frames will run whatever you put inside it sixty times. Today's field is the memory that turns that condition into an event.

Socratic: Choosing a Timing Model

  1. Trace your own 3.2 build. If the player stood inside the radius for one second at 60 frames per second, how many projectile clones did Instantiate create — and which line of your code is responsible for that number?
  2. Why can't you just call a "wait one second" function inside Update()? Describe what the player would see on screen during that wait, and explain why a game engine refuses to let you block the frame.
  3. Row (a) stores a moment; row (b) stores a duration. Which one can you print in the Console and have a player immediately understand, and which one is easier to compare against a designer's tuning value?
  4. Read the docs for InvokeRepeating. It has no idea where the player is. What has to move inside your firing method if you choose row (c), and what happens if you forget?
  5. Row (d) is described as the tool for sequences rather than single actions. What behaviour in this game is a sequence rather than a single action — and which state machine do you think the boss in Unit 8 will need?
  6. Which of the four approaches lets a designer change the fire rate from the Inspector without touching code? Which of them makes that rate hard to change while the game is running?
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Read each snippet for what it does in isolation, then work out how it maps onto your turret. None of these is from a video game.

Example 1 — A traffic signal honouring a minimum green time:

// The signal may not change until the clock has passed the minimum green window
bool maySwitch = Time.time >= greenStartedAt + minimumGreen;

Example 2 — A lighthouse counting down the dark between flashes:

// The lamp counts the darkness down; at zero it flashes and refills the counter
darkTimer -= Time.deltaTime;
if (darkTimer <= 0f) { Flash(); darkTimer = flashInterval; }

Example 3 — A bakery conveyor glazing on a fixed cadence:

// Repeats one action on a schedule the engine holds, not the machine
InvokeRepeating(nameof(SprayGlaze), 0f, 1.5f);

Example 4 — A stadium scoreboard running a timed sequence:

// Yield hands the frame back to the engine, then resumes this method later
IEnumerator Announce() { yield return new WaitForSeconds(3f); ShowScore(); }

Example 5 — A pedestrian crossing button (comment only):

// A second press inside the debounce window is discarded, not queued.
// The button remembers WHEN it was last pressed, not how many presses it owes.

Predict Before Building

  1. In Example 1, greenStartedAt was set to 12.0 and minimumGreen is 4.0. What is the earliest value of Time.time at which maySwitch becomes true?
  2. Example 1 compares against Time.time and Example 2 subtracts Time.deltaTime. Both measure a gap. Which one keeps working if the clock's meaning is different from frame count — and which one is tied to how often the frame runs?
  3. Example 3 never asks whether anything is in range. If you copied that shape into your turret exactly, what would the turret do while the player is on the other side of the map?
  4. Example 5 says the button remembers when, not how many. Which row of the timing table is that, and what does that tell you about the field you are about to add?
  5. In Example 2, what happens if darkTimer is declared inside the method that runs each frame instead of as a field on the class? What value does it hold at the start of the next frame?
Build Lab: Rate-Limit Your Turret ~25 min

Open Assets/Scripts/TurretController.cs — the file you built in 3.1 and 3.2. Everything you need is already there: a range knob, a cached target, a distance test, and a firing method that spawns a projectile from the muzzle. What is missing is one field and one condition.

Architectural specification for the cooldown:

The knob:

  • What serialized float lets a designer set the gap between shots from the Inspector without recompiling? What do you name it — and what does the name have to make obvious to a stranger reading your Inspector?
  • What default value will you ship? Justify it against the size of the Overworld and how fast your player moves. There is no correct answer in the project — there is only the answer you can defend.

The memory:

  • Which row of the table did you choose, and what single field does that row require? What type is it, and where does it live — inside Update() or on the class?
  • What should that field's starting value be so the turret can fire on the very first frame the player enters range? What happens to the first shot if you seed it wrongly?
  • If you chose the countdown, which line decrements the field, and does that line belong inside the range check or outside it? Argue both and pick.

The gate:

  • Which two conditions must both be true before the turret may fire? Which boolean operator expresses "both"?
  • Where exactly does the second condition attach to the range check you already wrote? Does the cooldown test belong inside the range test, or beside it?
  • Read the docs on && and short-circuit evaluation. If the player is out of range, does Unity bother evaluating the cooldown half at all?

The reset:

  • What line must run at the instant the turret actually fires? Which of your fields does it change, and to what?
  • Predict what happens if you omit it, before you test. You have already seen that bug once today.

Proving it:

  • How do you report each shot to the Console so you can count the cadence without a UI? What would you time with a stopwatch to check the number?

Wire nothing new in the Inspector beyond your own knob. Save, press Play, and stand inside the radius. Count the Console lines for ten seconds and compare them against your knob. If you get ten lines at a two-second cooldown, the gate works.

Bug Hunt: Timer Faults

  1. Comment out the line that records the new firing time. Step into range. What does the Console look like after one second, and which earlier lesson's bug have you just rebuilt?
  2. Set your cooldown knob to 0.5 in the Inspector and test again. How many shots per second is that, and at what point does the encounter stop being hard and start being unfair?
  3. Seed your timestamp field with a large value such as 100f. How long must the player stand in range before the very first shot — and what does that tell you about what the field actually means?
  4. Set the cooldown to 0. Is a zero-second cooldown different from no cooldown at all? Which one still protects your frame budget, and which one is the bug you started with?
  5. If you chose InvokeRepeating: walk out of range mid-burst. Are projectiles still being created? Who owns the timing in that design, you or the engine?
  6. If you chose the countdown: move the decrement line inside the range check and walk out of range for ten seconds. What is the timer's value when you walk back in, and how long until the next shot?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Choosing Between Timers

  1. Build the countdown version as well, so you can swap between two of the table's rows in the same script. Which one could you read and predict correctly after three weeks away from the project?
  2. Now imagine the turret has to charge for one second before each shot, fire three shots 0.15 seconds apart, then rest for two seconds. Which row of the table makes that sequence easy, and which two make it painful? Write the answer down — you will need it for the boss.
  3. Print the remaining time (or the elapsed time) to the Console every frame while the turret waits. Which of the two styles gives you a number that reads as a countdown a player would understand?
  4. Every system that runs in Update() performs its action once per frame. Which two places in your game is that correct for — and which system in Unit 4 will you have to decide about?
  5. Commit and push: "3.3: turret fire rate + cooldown".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why your turret was firing once per frame, naming the line responsible
  • Compare the four timing approaches and state what each one costs
  • Say which approach you chose, and give a reason that is about this behaviour
  • Explain why the reset line is mandatory, and what bug returns without it
  • Construct a compound boolean condition with && and explain short-circuit evaluation
  • Tune your cooldown knob in the Inspector and describe the change in pacing
  • Commit and push
